title: Composition over inheritance
idea: Composition over inheritance means a class gets behaviour by holding objects (has-a) and calling them, not by extending a parent (is-a).

analogy.text: A shop hires a courier firm rather than becoming one. It can switch couriers tomorrow, and customers still see only the shop counter.
analogy.breaks: In code, every forwarded call is a method you write.

points: Extending a class makes every public parent method part of your API.
A private field plus forwarding methods exposes only the calls you choose.
Type the field as an interface, so constructor injection can swap behaviour.
Interviewers expect has-a by default; justify each `extends` with a true is-a.

steps.caption: `AuditedStock` extends `ArrayList` and overrides `add` to write an audit line.
It also inherits `addAll`, `set`, `removeIf` and the rest. None of them pass through its `add`.
`Stock` holds the list as a private field. Callers cannot reach it.
Its few methods forward to the list and always record the change.
The audit is an `AuditSink` field. `Stock` knows the role, not the class.
Pass `MemoryAudit` in tests and a file-backed sink later. `Stock` does not change.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: Extending `ArrayList` to add an audit rule. Most changes skip the rule.

walk.text: The goal is an audit line per change. Extending `ArrayList` looks like the shortest path.
Only `add` is overridden. The class now relies on the parent calling it.
`addAll` in `ArrayList` copies the batch directly, so two items skip the override.
`set` and `removeIf` are inherited public methods too. Each changes the data with no audit.
The list and the audit disagree. Nothing failed to compile, so review is the only guard.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: `Stock` has a list and an `AuditSink`. Every change goes through one path.

walk.text: `AuditSink` names the role `Stock` needs. Any implementation can fill it.
The list is private and the sink arrives by constructor injection, checked for null.
`add` validates, stores and records. `addAll` reuses `add`, so no path skips the audit.
`remove` records only a real removal, so the trail matches the data.
`items` returns a read-only copy. Callers cannot edit the list behind the class.
The attempt to edit the copy fails, proving the backdoor is closed.

pitfalls: Extending `ArrayList` or `HashMap` to add a rule: inherited methods bypass it silently.
Typing the field as a concrete class keeps the coupling; type it as an interface.
Wrapping a true is-a type adds forwarding code and buys no flexibility.

quiz.q: Same `AuditedStock` as above. What does this print?
quiz.why: `ArrayList.addAll` copies the batch without calling `add`. Only `add("C")` runs the override, so three items but one audit line.

takeaway: Hold what you need behind an interface; extend only for true is-a.

starters: How do I tell a true is-a relationship from a convenient one?
